item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How Israel's war on Lebanon's water has become existential
item.description:
How Israel's war on Lebanon's water has become existential

Submitted by Zaynab Mayladan on Mon, 11/02/2026 - 19:08
Across the country's south, where water infrastructure has been targeted for decades, the ongoing conflict raises a key question: can life here ever get back to normal?
Insaf Faour and her granddaughter, Fatima, are pictured in August 2026 at their home in Debaal, Lebanon, which has been hit hard in Israel’s war (MEE/Zaynab Mayladan)
Off

It was half past five in the afternoon when Bahij Abdallah saw a white object pass overhead.

He was outside a pumping station in Ebel el-Saqi, in the hills above Marjayoun, checking on an open water reservoir. He had sat down on a stone step with his phone in his hand, while three colleagues remained inside. 

At first, he thought the white thing was a drone.

“Suddenly, it stopped in the air for a second, turned, and fell on the station,” Abdallah told Middle East Eye. “Then the smoke and the fire started.”

The phone flew out of his hand. He felt a wall of air, and then metal pushing into his body. He looked down and saw blood dripping from his face. His shoulder was burning. When he stood up, he saw that his shoe had been cut open. 

Abdallah, an electrical maintenance employee with the South Lebanon Water Establishment (SLWE), the state utility that supplies drinking water to two governorates, had been doing what he does most days: running the station and monitoring it. 

The facility is well known in the region and clearly marked, he said. “There are signs, and vehicles with the name and logo on them, that it belongs to the South Lebanon Water Establishment, which is a government body. And we were wearing the work uniform.”

The attack occurred on 9 June 2026, five days after Israel and the Lebanese government announced in Washington that they had agreed to a ceasefire. 

'I could have died in seconds. And I wasn't doing anything wrong; I was only pumping water for people to drink'

- Bahij Abdallah, state utility worker

Abdallah was taken to hospital where he underwent operations for severed tendons in his leg and shrapnel in his chest and shoulder. He spent two days in intensive care. He still walks slowly, cannot run, and is undergoing physiotherapy. 

His colleagues were not injured, and the station itself kept running; the damage was structural rather than technical, hitting an office and storage room.

Days later, the Lebanese army announced that a specialist unit had dismantled an unexploded guided aerial bomb inside the same water treatment station. 

“The station is rural,” Abdallah said. “There are no houses near it, or anything else.”

He has not gone back to work.

“It’s honestly not safe to go there anymore,” he said. “I could have died in seconds. And I wasn’t doing anything wrong. I was only pumping water for people to drink.”

'If we don't provide water, they won't return'

In the largest return movement of the war, more than 823,000 people have gone back to southern Lebanon in recent months, according to the United Nations humanitarian affairs office (Ocha), as the fragile ceasefire has remained in place. Some 334,000 remain displaced. 

In its assessments of the areas where people are returning, Ocha has consistently listed water and electricity as the services most frequently reported missing. A family can clear its own rubble and patch its own roof, but it cannot rebuild a pumping station, or re-lay two kilometres of a main utility line, or clean an aquifer. 

The scale of what has been lost is set out in an assessment published in July by the SLWE, covering two rounds of war between 2024 and 2026. It counts 175 reservoirs damaged, along with 16 main pumping stations, 124 wells and boreholes, nine springs, 104 chlorination systems, 85 generators, and more than 2,500 kilometres of pipe. 

The state utility puts the associated costs at more than $550m, and the number of people affected at more than 700,000. Restoring these systems will take years.

The SLWE, which is meant to do the rebuilding, has itself been hollowed out. Twenty-six of its employees have been killed by Israel since the war began, according to director general Wassim Daher, while its subscriber base has dwindled by around a third, representing a revenue collapse as much as a population statistic. 

Unlike electricity or telecommunications, water in Lebanon is not centrally administered; the SLWE is effectively the only public institution in this sector that is still operating across the south. 

Daher describes as a system strangled. More than 80 percent of its operating problems come down to the absence of electricity: the generators cannot run for more than five hours, the stations need 12, and the national grid does not reach many of the villages to which people have returned. 

“If we don’t provide water, they won’t return,” he told MEE. 

But to read the past three years as an isolated war on water is to miss what has been happening for the past century. Long before the current conflict, Israel has been diverting and destroying Lebanon’s water systems.

A century of war on water 

In 1919, as the region was gradually being reshaped in the aftermath of World War I, the Zionist movement submitted a document to the Paris Peace Conference proposing that Palestine’s border with Lebanon extend north of Sidon. This would put the basin of the Litani River inside the state it intended to establish on Palestinian soil.

“Israel considers its essential war to be the war over water resources,” Riad al-Assaad, a Lebanese civil engineer who has spent years mapping the south, told MEE. 

The Hasbani, a tributary of the Jordan River that flows through Lebanon, the occupied Golan Heights and northern Israel, “is the main theft Israel has committed”, Assaad said. 

What makes it valuable is practical: the Wazzani Spring, an integral part of the Hasbani, runs cold all year and rises high enough to descend under gravity, with no pumping, straight towards occupied Palestine. 

A history of Israel’s invasions of Lebanon
Read More »

Attempts to stop Israel’s water theft have all ended the same way.

In 1953, US envoy Eric Johnston was sent to divide the Jordan basin among the states that share it. He ultimately allotted Lebanon 35 million cubic metres a year, against 400 million for Israel, 480 million for Jordan and 132 million for Syria.

Lebanon rejected the plan as unjust, and did not manage to take even that; to this day, its use of the Hasbani has never exceeded one-fifth of the share Johnston gave it, according to expert assessments. 

After the Arab summit of 1964 resolved to control the Jordan’s headwaters - to stop Israel from drawing them south to the Negev - Israel destroyed the installations of the Hasbani-Wazzani diversion works inside Lebanon, and did the same in Syria. In the 1967 war, it seized key border water sources.

In 2002, after Lebanon rebuilt a modest pumping station at the Wazzani to supply border villages, Ariel Sharon, then Israel’s prime minister, called it a cause for war. The station was eventually allowed to open, with speeches about recovering Lebanon’s water wealth, but the message was clear: Lebanon could take what it needed, not what it was owed. 

“And until now, we are barely taking what we need. Let alone our right,” Assaad said. 

Professor Ahmad el-Hajj, an expert in hydrology and water management, has spent two months mapping the effects of the current war. He has recorded 12 kilometres of the Hasbani-Wazzani system under Israeli military occupation, with the Wazzani infrastructure destroyed. 

Of around 155 million cubic metres a year of surface water in that basin, he said, Lebanon was previously benefitting from four: “Now it is zero.” 

The crucial riverbend

The Litani runs 120 kilometres down the length of Lebanon from the Bekaa Valley, then turns sharply west below Beaufort Castle and heads to the sea. It is the one major river that is entirely Lebanese, from source to mouth.

At the bend sits a treatment and pumping station that supplies the villages of Jabal Amel. It was built when the UN Interim Force in Lebanon first deployed in the late 1970s, in country so steep there were no roads to it; the pipes were carried in by helicopter and pack animals, Assaad said. 

“At this exact point, it is the closest thing to Palestine,” he said, citing a distance of fewer than three kilometres. “Israel has coveted this bend, this exact spot, for its entire life.” 

Assaad added: “Whoever says Israel doesn’t need water is wrong. Yes, it desalinates 600 million cubic metres [annually]. Yes, it is the most important state in the world for recycling wastewater. But with its settlement expansion, it needs water permanently.”

Before it was destroyed, the Wazzani infrastructure supplied, directly or indirectly, around 42 villages, including a pumping station in Markaba that was hit this past July in what the UN flagged as a case of civilian infrastructure being targeted. 

The villages that drank from these systems - such as Khiam, Kfar Kila, Odaisseh, Houla and Blida - appeared in satellite analysis published by Israeli media earlier this year with more than 80 percent of their buildings destroyed. 

Nasser Nasrallah, who once led the Litani River National Authority and now heads a local NGO focused on sustainable development, told MEE that a multimillion-dollar project to bring Litani water to southern villages - more than two-thirds of which had been built before the war - was derailed by the conflict.

He added: “Because Israel came in with war these two years and wrecked the project, the project was delayed - and we are losing.”

In late October, the Litani authority filed a criminal complaint against Israel with the public prosecutor in Nabatieh over the pollution of the river. It has been referred to local police for further investigation.

Pattern of destruction

What has emerged in recent months is an ominous pattern: facilities that were rebuilt with the help of aid groups after the 2024 escalation have been decimated again in the current war.

In Debaal, in Tyre district, a well and solar array that served around 5,800 people was rehabilitated by the Norwegian Refugee Council after the 2024 war, with the project completed by the end of last year, according to municipal officials. Within months, it was destroyed again in a direct Israeli strike. 

“The water situation in the village was better before the war,” Haydar Fawaz, the deputy head of the municipal council, told MEE. “Now one station needs electricity and another needs maintenance, and families are buying trucked water they never used to buy.”

In nearby Froun, a reservoir was destroyed this past March, along with the solar system powering the village’s well, which served nearly 3,000 people. Mohammad Makki, who heads the municipality’s displacement and disaster committee, told MEE that more than 270 solar panels had been installed by an aid organisation in 2025, as part of a $70,000 initiative to revamp the local energy system; that project has now been severely set back. 

'In at least several incidents the damaged or destroyed facilities were located in large open areas without clearly identifiable military targets'

- Report by Oxfam and other monitoring groups

Meanwhile, in Debel, a Christian village in Bint Jbeil district, one resident - who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of Israeli repercussions - told MEE that after Israeli forces hit the public water network earlier this year, the village had no supply for more than two weeks, during which time people fell back on private wells. 

Surveillance footage later showed Israeli soldiers destroying the solar array that powered the village’s water system. Months later, the resident said, “the system has still not been repaired”. 

The pattern of destruction extends far beyond these three villages. This past March, Oxfam noted that Israeli forces were hitting water and sanitation infrastructure across southern Lebanon, including by dropping bombs “near sites that were being rehabilitated after having been destroyed or damaged in the last war”.

Of the 19 water facilities that Oxfam and its partners were responsible for rehabilitating - infrastructure serving up to 60,000 people - six were damaged in 2025, the organisation noted. 

A report last year by Oxfam, Action Against Hunger and the monitoring group Insecurity Insight documented at least 26 pumping stations and 28 pipeline networks damaged or destroyed across southern Lebanon. 

“In at least several incidents the damaged or destroyed facilities were located in large open areas without clearly identifiable military targets,” the report stated, citing significant damage to the Wazzani system and the associated Maisat water pumping station, which serves around 150,000 people across 30 towns and villages.

Insecurity Insight has since logged at least a dozen further incidents. Its director, Christina Wille, told New Lines Magazine that the repetition “points to a pattern”, suggesting “a deliberate strategy rather than isolated or incidental damage”.

Naji Kehdy, a Lebanese researcher in hydrogeology, told MEE that looking at the types of facilities hit proves nothing by itself. What raises the probability of deliberate targeting is the pattern, including repeated damage to the small, specific components that keep water systems functioning (such as solar panels, chlorination units and pumps); the targeting of facilities that are nowhere near military sites; and the precision and repetition of strikes on water infrastructure.

Under international humanitarian law, drinking-water installations are civilian objects that are supposed to have special protections. 

Back in Ebel el-Saqi, Abdallah notes how high the costs have become in his line of work. One colleague was killed by an Israeli air strike en route to his job, while a municipal councillor and a municipal employee in Kfarshuba were abducted by Israeli forces while switching on the village water station.

“Our work is very dangerous,” Abdallah said. “We’re carrying our lives in our hands.”

Exacerbated by drought

The destruction has arrived at the worst possible time. 

Lebanon is in what the Litani River Authority describes as its most significant drought in more than 65 years, with close to 90 percent of Lebanon’s springs dried up. According to the Red Cross, the vast majority of Lebanese households are in a state of moderate to high water insecurity, with millions of people facing severe shortages.

The effects of drought and broken pipes compound each other, Kehdy said. Less rain means less water soaking back into the ground, which means lower water tables and weaker springs. Broken infrastructure means less public water. Both push people towards private wells, lowering the water table further.

On the coast, pumping too hard can pull seawater into coastal aquifers, a problem that can persist for years after the rain returns and pipes are fixed.

Living on pavements, bathing in the sea: Lebanon's displaced face winter without shelter
Read More »

When there is less water, whatever is in it becomes more concentrated. In Lebanon, the National Council for Scientific Research recently tested 134 soil samples across the south and the Bekaa Valley, and recorded several areas where the soil held far more phosphorus than it should, “suggesting possible links to white phosphorus munitions”. Chromium, which can be toxic, exceeded safe agricultural limits in nearly half the samples. 

The contaminated land is not comprised of empty hillsides. It contains olive groves, orchards, tobacco fields and irrigated ground. The study counted more than 8,200 farmers directly affected, and some 654,000 people living in more than 200 villages in the area.

Hajj, the hydrology expert who has been mapping the crisis, said around two-thirds of the war zone sits over land that would quickly carry contaminants into the groundwater supply. But his map is one of risk: it indicates where samples should urgently be taken, not where contamination has been proven. A systematic groundwater sampling process, following the contours of his map, has not taken place. 

The SLWE’s own assessment warns that explosions may open new fractures in rock surfaces, change how groundwater moves, and weaken springs, while explosive residues, heavy metals, hydrocarbons and rocket fuel “may migrate rapidly through South Lebanon’s karst aquifers”. 

Daher, the water establishment’s director general, is blunter about the limits of what is known. His teams test for certain things, but without knowing what Israel is dropping, they are not necessarily testing for the right things. What really worries him is the risk that various contaminants are going undetected. 

Soil testing falls to the agriculture ministry, while water testing belongs to the water establishment. Nobody compiles the results in one place, SLWE officials told MEE. 

According to Kehdy, without the necessary testing being done, it is impossible to determine whether or how significantly local groundwater has been contaminated by Israel’s wars.

If a limestone aquifer is contaminated by heavy metals, it is effectively impossible to clean because of the deep cracks that can’t be flushed out, Kehdy said. Money and time can fix water pipes; they cannot restore a devastated aquifer.

Villages empty

In Froun, the village pond is full. 

It is as old as the village itself, dating back to its roots as a tiny farming community. Everyone here has memories attached to it: swimming in the pond, drawing water from it, washing dishes at its edge, carrying water home on donkeys, irrigating mint. A plaque by the pond notes that it was restored a decade ago with Italian funding and money from Lebanon’s reconstruction council. Filled from rainfall and road runoff, it survived the war.

This year, its water level is unusually high - and not because of rain.

“The situation would actually be different if agriculture was still active,” said Makki, the head of the local disaster committee. “The pond would probably be dry, because people would draw the water for irrigation. Since there are no longer many farms, the water remains here for longer.”

According to Makki, Froun lost around 27 of its usual 30 tonnes of honey in the 2024-25 season, as beekeepers couldn’t reach their hives, and the bees died or dispersed for lack of water. The goats that were shipped off daily for meat production disappeared, along with the seven butchers’ shops. Tobacco fields went thirsty. Olive trees went unharvested, the fruit coated in dust.

A pond stays full when there is nobody left to empty it. 

Thirteen kilometres away, Insaf Faour, an 80-year-old resident of Debaal, describes a similar phenomenon. Decades ago, even when other villages had to purchase water, Debaal could rely on its own natural resources. In recent years, however, households have been buying two or three tanker loads a season amid severe drought conditions, she said.

This year, they stopped. 

'When you lose your house, you lose your memories and the beautiful things with them'

- Abeer, displaced resident of Kfarsir

“We didn’t buy, because water is available,” Faour told MEE. “Because there are fewer houses.”

Dozens of the village’s housing units have been destroyed since 2024. With fewer homes, there are fewer people, and more water to go around.

A study published in July by the Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies, based on eight focus groups with 64 people who had recently returned to their homes in southern Lebanon, drew a distinction that the headline numbers can obscure: going back to a place is not the same as being able to live in it. Spatial return means resuming residence in a house or town; sustainable return requires the restored capacity to live, plan, work, invest and stay. Many participants were suspended between the two.

“We went back, but we are not reassured,” one study participant said.

Some of those surveyed said water was available, while others said there was none at all. That divergence, the researchers concluded, showed why conditions must be assessed at the level of the individual neighbourhood and town, rather than through general indicators. 

The study concluded: “The success of return should not be measured solely by the number of families who have returned or the number of houses repaired, but by families’ capacity for permanent stability and the restoration of normal life.”

What disappears with the water

From the age of seven or eight, Faour recalls carrying water home from the village spring in Debaal, walking alongside her mother. She continued relying on the spring after she married, bathing her children there, doing laundry, meeting neighbours and chatting while jars filled. 

When the spring ran low in the daytime, women would go at night and wait, each in turn, to fill a jar. But the water ultimately stopped flowing after a municipal well was drilled above the spring.

Fawaz, the municipal official, remembers a lake he swam in as a boy. It was shelled in 2006, again in 2024, and once again this year. His recollections suddenly bring to mind another, older lake, abandoned and built over sometime after the year 2000.

“When something disappears,” he said, “the memory disappears with it.”

Abeer, a resident of nearby Kfarsir, has been living in a school shelter in Beirut for seven months with her four children. Her house is gone, along with her husband’s car, and there is neither electricity nor water in what remains of their village. 

“I don’t want to go back and see the situation in the village,” she told MEE. “I still haven’t visited, because I don’t want to see it like this.”

What she grieves is specific: a mulberry tree her mother planted in front of the family home, 30 years old, and large enough to shade the whole building. She drank her coffee under it, ate breakfast under it, and gossiped with family members there. 

'At our river, there are trees that grew by themselves, wild apples, the taste of syrup. Nobody planted them. But now Israel deprived us of the river'

- Abeer, resident of Kfarsir

It was destroyed in Israeli attacks, along with their garden: “When you lose your house, you lose your memories and the beautiful things with them.”

She also grieves her loss of access to the Litani River where it runs past her village, near Qaaqiyet al-Jisr.

“At our river, there are trees that grew by themselves, wild apples, the taste of syrup. Nobody planted them. But now Israel deprived us of the river,” Abeer said.

“We used to go down to it every Sunday. The whole family would gather; one brings fruits, one brings watermelon, one brings meat, and we’d grill it. We’d sit under the trees beside the water, with the watermelon cooling in the middle of the river.”

Earlier this year, a video circulated of Israeli women swimming in the Hasbani River in southern Lebanon. 

“When I saw the video, I was fuming,” Abeer said. “They are swimming in our river when we are not allowed to go there anymore.”

Israeli companies linked to Gaza genocide to head to India for tech summits

Submitted by Azad Essa on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 08:41
Suppliers of drones, military sensors and surveillance technology are among 45 Israeli companies expected at events in Hyderabad and Bengaluru
An Israeli soldier takes position at a checkpoint in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on 23 October 2026 (Ahmad Gharabali/AFP)
Off

Several Israeli firms whose military equipment has been used in the genocidal war on Gaza are heading to India later this month to explore partnerships with local firms, Middle East Eye can reveal.

Twenty Israeli companies are expected to attend a start-up event in Hyderabad, Telangana, on 16 November, organised by T-Hub, which describes itself as "the world's largest startup hub", supporting founders through programmes, partnerships and access to global markets.

A further 25 Israeli companies are expected at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, billed as Asia's premier platform for technology, commerce and innovation, which runs from 17 to 19 November.

The companies include XTEND, whose drones have been deployed by Israeli forces in Gaza, including one allegedly used to track and film the killing of Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar on 16 October 2024. 

Also attending are Dagan-Optics, a supplier of equipment to Israeli military units, and Netzer Precision, whose sensors are incorporated into Israeli tanks and armoured personnel carriers.

The summits are intended to provide opportunities for technological collaboration and commercial partnerships between Israeli tech companies and local firms.

An MEE analysis of the companies scheduled to attend has found that several are either directly involved in Israel's military operations in Gaza or materially connected to the country's wider military-industrial complex, including its occupation infrastructure in the occupied West Bank.

'India's police and investigative agencies are buying surveillance and forensic tools from abroad faster than Parliament is writing rules for them'

- IFF spokesperson

At least 250,000 Palestinians have been killed or injured over the past three years, with more than 1,600 killed since a so-called ceasefire went into effect in October 2025.

The events come at a sensitive time in India, following revelations by the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) that the central government and several state governments had cleared to purchase mobile phone extraction technology from Israeli firm Cellebrite.

Cellebrite technology is reported to have been used to extract information from Palestinians detained by Israel, many of whom have been tortured.

The company also has a record of its technology being used by governments around the world to access devices belonging to activists and journalists.

India has witnessed a wave of protests in recent months, and activists fear authorities may have used the technology to unlawfully extract data from the phones of people detained during demonstrations.

The IFF investigation also found that states governed by the main opposition Congress party had purchased the technology, underscoring the bipartisan nature of India's ties with Israel.

"India's police and investigative agencies are buying surveillance and forensic tools from abroad faster than Parliament is writing rules for them," an IFF spokesperson told MEE.

"In India, the people on whom such tools get used first are protesters, journalists, Kashmiris and Adivasi communities, because they have the least ability to find out and push back," the spokesperson said.

Complicity in genocide

The summits scheduled for mid-November are the latest in a series of interactions between the business communities of India and Israel, spanning electronics, technology and cyber security, since the genocide began in October 2023.

The events will showcase a broad range of Israeli companies working in artificial intelligence, robotics, semiconductors and defence technology, several of which have links to Israel's military operations in Gaza.

Dagan-Optics, which manufactures thermal imaging and targeting equipment, has said it donated products to the Israeli military, including armoured units, paratroopers and infantry.

"In return, we only asked for feedback and opinions about the products from the users," the company's founder, Rafael Dagan, said in an advertorial published in Haaretz in August 2024.

XTEND, meanwhile, has supplied the small drones deployed by Israeli forces in Gaza.

Several reports have claimed that XTEND drones were used to track down Sinwar and film him during his final moments.

Reuters reported in January 2025 that XTEND was "one of many to get a boost from Israel's war needs".

Months later, Israel's Defence Ministry Procurement Directorate announced that the company had won a tender to "supply thousands of FPV (first person view) drones to the IDF Ground Forces".

Another firm heading to India, Netzer Precision, has supplied sensors for several Israeli weapons systems, including Merkava tanks used in Gaza, as well as armoured personnel carriers.

According to an advert, Merkava tanks, considered Israel's premier tank, have been used "in urban raids and to support infantry in densely built environments where ambushes, improvised explosive devices (IEDs), and anti-tank threats are constant".

All three companies are scheduled to attend both the Hyderabad event and the Bengaluru summit, which is organised by Karnataka's Department of Electronics, IT and Biotechnology among others.

MEE found that besides these three companies, several other firms with close links to Israel's military-industrial complex and occupation infrastructure will also participate.

These include: Jeen.ai, an AI software company that provides critical AI infrastructure to the Israeli security establishment; Orca Security, a cyber security firm that says 90 percent of its team has a military background; and Magal Solutions, an Israeli security and technology firm that installed intrusion detection systems and sensors along the fence around Gaza and sections of Israel's separation barrier in the occupied West Bank.

Magal has also been linked to the installation of sensors along the fence on the de-facto border with Pakistan in Indian-controlled Kashmir.

Another company making the trip is Ruby AI, a robotics firm that developed a "mechanical octopus" to clean Israeli army tanks.

The Jerusalem Post reported that the company was seeking to develop "a robot capable of performing a task that is extremely dangerous for a soldier: clearing underground tunnels".

Accelerating collaborations

Over the past three years, cooperation between India and Israel has extended beyond government departments and technology companies.

Several Israeli universities have also deepened ties with their Indian counterparts, as student-led campaigns at universities in the West have put pressure on academic institutions to sever links with Israel.

Second Israeli soldier accused of Gaza war crimes leaves India after complaint
Read More »

In March 2024, Indian Institute of Technology-Delhi and Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) signed an applied research agreement, while several other Indian Institutes of Technology across the country have continued discussions with Israeli institutions of higher education.

Meanwhile, thousands of Israelis continue to travel to India on holiday after completing their military service. Indian authorities were urged to initiate arrest proceedings against two former Israeli soldiers accused of war crimes in Gaza while holidaying in the country.

Both men subsequently left India, with New Delhi showing little interest in pursuing the allegations.

The Indian government and the private sector have also been implicated in supplying weapons to Israel during the genocide.

In July, Amnesty International documented at least 2,596 shipments of weapons, ammunition, parts and components exported from India to Israel between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025. 

"Before any Indian agency signs with these vendors, it should publish what it is buying, the law it relies on to use it, and who will audit that use," the spokesperson with the IFF added.

"At the moment none of those three things exists."

MEE reached out to T-Hub, XTEND, Dagan-Optics, Netzer Precision, Magal Solutions and the organisers of the Bengaluru Tech Summit for comment, but did not receive a response by time of publication.

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.

After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Exclusive: Toyota reviewing use of forklifts by Israeli military after MEE investigation
item.description:
Exclusive: Toyota reviewing use of forklifts by Israeli military after MEE investigation

Submitted by Sebastian Shehadi on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 15:16
Manufacturer reviewing whether 'civil-use' clause breached after MEE uncovers Israeli defence ministry contract and use of forklifts at munitions sites and army bases
An image of a Toyota forklift at a missiles and ammunition centre in northern Israel, as posted on Israeli military social media accounts on 7 July. (Facebook)
On

Toyota has said it is investigating the use of its forklifts by the Israeli military after Middle East Eye found photos and videos of the vehicles at weapons and munitions storage sites, serving supply lines for frontline units, and being used by the army’s Logistics Corps.

It comes after MEE uncovered details of a previously unreported 158m-shekel ($49.8m) contract between Toyota and Israel’s Ministry of Defense for the supply of forklifts that was signed in 2024 – the first full year of the Gaza war.

Toyota says that its vehicles are not intended for military use.

When asked about the contract, the company told MEE it had commitments in place with both the defence ministry and its official reseller in Israel to ensure that its technology and products were “for civil use only”.

But when MEE then shared footage posted on official Israeli military social media channels, which showed Toyota forklifts being used at locations including a missiles and ammunition depot in northern Israel, a Logistics Corps training base, and inside a munitions factory, it said it was investigating the images to determine whether those agreements had been breached.

Toyota is a Japanese corporation but its main forklift business, Toyota Material Handling, is headquartered in the United States.

"While it is impossible for any vehicle maker to track vehicles that may have been bought and resold by intermediaries, we are reviewing these photos and videos and are investigating whether our use agreements have been violated," a spokesperson for Toyota Material Handling told MEE.

'If necessary, we will take action to prevent unauthorized or inappropriate use of our forklifts'

- Toyota Material Handling

"If necessary, we will take action to prevent unauthorized or inappropriate use of our forklifts."

Arms industry experts told MEE that any such action could lead Toyota to suspend sales to Israel – while noting that the company’s initial acceptance of Israeli assurances that its equipment would not be put to military use, at a time when Israeli forces were facing mounting accusations of war crimes, raised questions about the robustness of its due diligence processes.

"It is true that we cannot expect companies to track their vehicles after the initial sale,” said Noam Perry, strategic research coordinator at the American Friends Service Committee, a Quaker organisation in the US that researches companies supplying the Israeli military.

"However, this is a multi-million-dollar contract delivered directly to the Israeli Ministry of Defense at a time when it is accused of committing war crimes. Any due diligence process should have raised questions about the use of these forklifts."

The Israeli defence ministry declined to comment.

'Contractual commitments'

Toyota’s sale of forklifts to Israel was revealed in a budget report for 2024, quietly published by the finance ministry’s accountant general in March 2025 and hitherto unreported, which listed the defence ministry’s largest procurement commitments for the year.

MEE can find no evidence that the contract was publicised at the time it was signed by either the defence ministry or Toyota.

An entry in the report headed “Purchase of forklifts” reads: “An engagement from 2024, valued at approximately NIS 158 million, with Toyota for the purchase of heavy-duty forklifts. The remaining balance of the engagement as of 31 December, 2024, is approximately NIS 158 million, and it is expected to conclude in 2026.”

There is no further information about how many machines were bought, but new heavy forklifts can sell for roughly $80,000 or more depending on lifting capacity, which would mean an order of this size could add up to hundreds of vehicles.

The entry is listed in a section focused on military spending under the title “Land Platforms” – military parlance for vehicles used by ground forces – and appears between a 174m-shekel ($54.9m) contract with Israeli firm Plasan Sasa for armoured vehicles and a 120m-shekel ($37.8m) purchase of armoured diggers from the US Army.

When MEE contacted Toyota Material Handling with queries about the contract, the company said its machines were not intended for military purposes.

“Toyota Material Handling forklifts are designed for civil use, such as moving merchandise in a warehouse or cargo at a port," a spokesperson said. "We would never want or condone our equipment being used for anything beyond this."

The company went on to describe binding restrictions: "We have contractual commitments in place with both our reseller in Israel and the country's Ministry of Defense that our products and technologies will be for civil use only."

Toyota’s reseller in Israel is Union Industrial Vehicle Ltd, which sells its industrial equipment brands under a single distributorship. Union Industrial Vehicle Ltd did not respond to requests for comment.

Munitions on pallets

With support from Perry at the American Friends Service Committee, MEE then reviewed official Israeli military social media platforms and found photos and videos which appeared to show Toyota forklifts being used for military-related functions.

One image posted on the Instagram page of the Israeli army’s Technology and Maintenance Corps on 7 July showed a Toyota forklift carrying a pallet which appears to be loaded with munitions.

An accompanying caption reads: “A few small moments we caught from the intensive work of the missile and ammunition centre of the Northern District.”

Other images in the post show pallets stacked with 155mm artillery shells. 

The image may have been taken at the Ramat David airbase in northern Israel.

In June, the Israeli army’s Instagram and Facebook pages posted portraits of soldiers as part of an “appreciation month” campaign for reservists. Among them: a reservist major “combat manager” at the wheel of a Toyota forklift.

According to the Facebook post accompanying the photo, the combat manager had completed more than 500 reserve days "in the unit responsible for the production and supply of aircraft ammunition at Ramat David base".

Another Instagram post, dated 3 March 2024 and this time posted by the army’s Logistics Corps, showed photos of soldiers, some carrying rifles, gathered around a Toyota forklift at the Logistics Corps' Bahad 6 training base.

The Logistics Corps, the caption said, was working with the army's driving administration to continue running forklift driver training courses despite the war, including in the frontline units.

Meanwhile, a photograph posted in March this year via Kol Hahayalim, an Israeli army Instagram account, shows a Toyota forklift lifting storage drums from the back of a lorry, a soldier at the controls.

The caption said the General Staff Supply Centre had issued “everything required for the IDF’s operational continuity” during Operation Roaring Lion – the US and Israeli attack on Iran – and set out what that meant: hundreds of tanker-loads of jet fuel, petrol and aviation petrol, 300 tonnes of lubricants, 70,000 spare parts for armoured fighting vehicles, 80,000 for optronic systems, and a thousand units of blood plasma.

The General Staff Supply Centre is located at the Tel Hashomer army base in central Israel.

Israel’s military has also highlighted the importance of forklifts in support of its operations, including during the mass mobilisation at the beginning of the war in Gaza in October 2023.

On 9 October, two days into the war, the IDF’s official Instagram account posted photographs of the operation to equip the 360,000 reservists it had just called up, including an image of a Toyota forklift with a military number plate loaded with a container of what appear to be soldiers’ helmets.

“We’re not short of equipment… Everything will arrive," the caption says. This equipment included 79,000 personal protection kits consisting of helmets and vests, according to the post.

The next day, the Israeli news website News08 published a photo of the same vehicle. It said the army had added "1,500 forklifts, trucks and pallet trucks" to its inventory of vehicles in addition to those already held by units.

MEE’s investigation uncovered another intriguing example, published by Israel’s Ministry of Defense itself, which draws attention to how some Toyota-manufactured forklifts have served the war effort.

In January 2024, the ministry posted a video on its YouTube channel under the title "Watch: how 'blue and white' shells are made".

It shows the tank and artillery shell production line at Elbit Systems, Israel's largest defence company. The line had run continuously since 7 October, the ministry said, and supplied large quantities of ammunition to the fighting forces.

Thirty-one seconds in, among the shell casings on the factory floor, stands an orange forklift, an Elbit worker in a hard hat beside it. The name on its counterweight is Toyota.

MEE understands that Toyota has now identified the forklift with records showing that the machine was sold by the company’s Israeli reseller four years ago to a civilian logistics and storage company, not to Elbit Systems. 

Toyota has no information about what became of it after that delivery – its location, use or ownership, or whether it was later sold or rented to another party, MEE understands.

Elbit Systems did not respond to requests for comment.

Maintenance contracts

While these photos and videos offer episodic evidence of the Israeli military’s use of Toyota equipment, the defense ministry’s own paperwork provides further details about the extent of the forklift fleet.

A public register of contracts awarded by the ministry without competitive tender includes entries totalling some $1.7m, dated 15 February 2024, for the “maintenance of Toyota forklifts throughout the IDF”. Other forklift brands appear in the register too.

Toyota forklifts were being used by Israeli military and policing institutions before the current war on Gaza.

In 2018, the MoD published a tender for the maintenance of Toyota forklifts for the Israeli Air Force, according to Who Profits, an Israeli research centre that documents corporate ties to the occupation.

'Any sale of equipment to the Israeli military, regardless of its specific uses, is supporting the IDF's activities. There is no ethical business to be done with the IDF, period'

-  Samuel Perlo-Freeman, Campaign Against Arms Trade

Who Profits records the Israeli police contracting Union Industrial Vehicle Ltd – Toyota’s Israeli distributor – in March 2022 to maintain and repair its forklifts.

An image of a Toyota forklift at the Nevatim airbase – the hub for the Israeli air force’s heavy transport planes – featured in an article published on the air force website in January 2023.

Israel's defence ministry does have civilian-facing arms. It runs rehabilitation and welfare services for wounded veterans, and a department for bereaved families and commemoration. However, the apparent role of forklifts in such departments appears limited. 

For this reason, Toyota's “civil-use” clause puzzles Perry, who leads the American Friends Service Committee’s Investigate project which documents corporate involvement in Israel’s occupation.

"Toyota cannot expect civil use only if they have a contract with [the Israeli defence ministry]," he told MEE. 

“The due diligence process, if done seriously, should have flagged a contract with a military in an active conflict zone for heightened scrutiny.”

Whatever “civil use” means in the contract, the commitment depends on someone establishing how the machines are used in practice. That duty falls on the seller, according to Samuel Perlo-Freeman, a researcher on the international arms trade at Campaign Against Arms Trade.

"Toyota can’t take Israeli assurances regarding the uses to which their equipment is put at face value, but should verify that they are not being used directly in illegal activities," Perlo-Freeman told MEE.

"If they cannot do this, then they risk complicity in such activities."

"[That said], any sale of equipment to the Israeli military, regardless of its specific uses, is supporting the IDF's activities. There is no ethical business to be done with the IDF, period."

Perlo-Freeman said he hoped Toyota would conduct a proper investigation and take appropriate action.

“With the prospect of West Bank settlement sanctions, civilian companies might be wanting to be a bit more cautious about their products being used in the Occupied Palestinian Territories," he said.

Vehicles requisitioned

Toyota has not shared details of its contract with the Israeli defence ministry, nor has it said what it would treat as a violation or what action it might take.

But if the “civil use” clause is clearly stated, and there is clear evidence of a breach, then “Toyota could presumably suspend sales”, Mark Bromley, who directs the dual-use and arms trade control programme at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told MEE.

But, even if Toyota is able to track where its machines ended up, there may be only so much heavy lifting its contract can do.

A civil-use clause would bind two parties: Toyota’s Israeli reseller and the defence ministry.

But it would only cover the machines Toyota sells into those arrangements. Every other forklift in Israel – the ones sold to private companies, working in warehouses and ports – falls outside them, and therefore within the scope of a separate power.

Under a 1987 Israeli law governing the registration and requisition of equipment for the military, the army can take privately owned equipment from the civilian economy for operational needs.

In the first month of the war in Gaza the army used that power on a scale unseen in years, requisitioning thousands of vehicles to move equipment and supplies.

What was taken was mainly trucks, commercial vehicles, forklifts and heavy engineering equipment, as Israeli business newspaper TheMarker reported in November 2023.

That process predated the 2024 contract. But a forklift working in a private Israeli warehouse is liable to be pressed into military service irrespective of anything the manufacturer has agreed with the defence ministry.

According to Perry though, Toyota has set itself a standard that should not depend on the contract at all.

Toyota Industries, the parent company of Toyota Material Handling and other subsidiaries, maintains a group human rights policy based on the United Nations’ Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.

More than 50 British MPs demand fresh sanctions on Israel over Gaza aid obstruction
Read More »

It commits the company to "establish and continuously implement a human rights due-diligence process to identify, prevent, mitigate negative impacts on human rights related to our corporate activities", and states that it expects business partners, including suppliers, to support the policy.

Those principles ask companies operating in conflict-affected areas to apply heightened due diligence.

For Perry, Toyota's adoption of that standard matters more than anything else the company has said: it makes the obligation one Toyota accepts rather than one urged on it from outside.

The obvious follow-up, in his view, is whether the company has carried out such an assessment for Israel – and whether it would publish what that assessment found.

MEE asked Toyota whether any such assessment was made before the 2024 contract but did not get an answer.

Perry called the investigation "a good first step in the right direction, for the company to acknowledge a potential oversight and to investigate further", whilst adding that Toyota Material Handling should immediately halt any pending shipments to Israel until its investigation is complete.

"It should publish the results of its investigation and take appropriate actions in accordance with the UN Guiding Principles for Business and Human Rights, which it says it is committed to.”

That, he said, meant "providing access to remedy to the people and communities whose human rights were negatively impacted", and amending the company's due-diligence process "to ensure that this kind of oversight does not happen again".

item.description:
Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand next round of negotiations to include European countries

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has warned against the EU agreeing to Russia’s proposed sequence of talks on Ukraine, saying it would allow Moscow to “divert the attention away” from its actions and ultimately leave Europe “in a worse place.”

She welcomed the US side “finally admitting what I said already one and a half years ago – that for any deal between Russia and Ukraine … you also need the Europeans.”

“I hope that we are just not at the table, but we are actually also really influencing the outcome of these negotiations.”

“The most important is that we keep to our agreement that first the ceasefire, then peace agreement and then any kind of other talks … when Russia is still presenting their maximum demands, then we should also stick to the maximum demands and start to negotiate from there. …

“If we walk into that trap that we start to discuss … the European security architecture, then I don’t think we are in a better place. We are actually in worse place.”

“Let’s focus on what it is at hand. We have one aggressor and one victim. The aggressor does not have security concerns, as nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”

“I know that the Russians don’t want me, but do we have a say on who is representing Russia? No, we don’t.”

“Well, we have institutions in place, so we can’t just send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending. Clearly, we should not copy the same patterns.”

“They don’t want [anyone] strong on the other side because they want to push their through their maximum demands, like they have always done. Because … their tactics is very clear: at first you present threats and ultimatums, you use force, and then you will just wait, because there will always be people in the west who will offer you something you didn’t have before. And every time you go further.

So, of course, if you negotiate with anybody, you want the other side to be as weak as possible so that you can get what you want.”

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] India clears Israeli firm Cellebrite to supply phone-hacking tools to government agencies
item.description:
India clears Israeli firm Cellebrite to supply phone-hacking tools to government agencies

India has exempted Israeli surveillance company Cellebrite from domestic procurement rules, allowing government agencies to purchase its phone-extraction and hacking technology, an investigation has found.

The digital-rights group Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) found that Home Minister Amit Shah approved a waiver for the National Investigation Agency (NIA), clearing the way for the purchase of at least 422 foreign forensic products, including Cellebrite tools.

The technology can extract data from seized devices and use recovered login tokens to access more than 100 cloud services, including social media platforms such as Instagram, X and Tinder. 

Digital-rights experts have warned that the expansion of surveillance capabilities raises serious privacy concerns, with India's existing laws offering inadequate safeguards against excessive monitoring.
